do_more: Focus topics around visceral human actions like 'play', physical body reactions (faces freezing, stomach knots, desk job movement), and immediate sensory responses.
Frame public-domain psychology concepts using direct 'Your' addressing ('Your Play', 'Your Brain', 'Your Screen Hours') to make historical texts immediately relatable.
Write short, punchy titles under 5 words that promise a simple personal benefit or state a startling observation.
Target tight video lengths (~30s) where average retention easily crosses 50-100% to push the video higher into the Shorts feed algorithm.
avoid: Abstract academic questions (e.g., 'Can thoughts shape reality?', 'Does your brain follow steps?') which feel theoretical and dry.
Academic citation titles or academic-sounding book titles (e.g., 'Psychology and Industrial Efficiency', 'The Analysis of Mind').
Overly broad historical or socio-economic angles like class consciousness, eugenics, or 19th-century blueprints.
short.title_style: High-performing titles are short, present-tense, ultra-direct statements starting with 'Your' or 'Why' that target an everyday physical or mental experience.
next_tests: Test 'Your Body Knows' frame: Pair classic Darwin emotional expressions with modern bodily experiences (e.g., 'Why your heart races when ignored').
Compare tight (~30s) vs standard (~42s) lengths using identical audio scripts on 'Your Play' or 'Your Screen Time' hooks to see which drives higher relative retention.

do_more: Start each script with a 30‑second hook that poses a vivid, curiosity‑driving question (e.g., "Why do you dream about falling?")
Feature a well‑known historical psychologist or thinker in the title and opening to leverage name recognition
Frame the topic as a personal, everyday dilemma that viewers can relate to (habits, dreams, choices)
Keep the overall video concise (just over 3 minutes) but ensure the core explanation is delivered clearly within the first minute
Use emotionally charged language (why, how, what if) to spark intrigue
avoid: Long, abstract titles without a clear question or hook
Overly academic or dense introductions that exceed 45 seconds
Repeating the same series format or phrasing that has been rejected
Neglecting to mention a recognizable figure or concrete example
full.title_style: Use a direct question or surprising statement that includes a famous psychologist's name, e.g., "Why do you dream about falling? | Sigmund Freud"
next_tests: Compare a 30‑second tight hook vs. a 42‑second standard hook on the same topic to measure watch‑through rate
Create two versions of a script: one featuring a famous figure in the title, another with a generic title, and track VPD
Experiment with adding a personal anecdote in the first 15 seconds to see if avgPercent improves
